claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a relatively coarse-grained microstructure.
Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a non-uniform distribution of protective alloying elements such as chromium.
Controlled thermal annealing of Q235 steel will produce a finer-grained microstructure than the unannealed state.
The finer-grained annealed microstructure will have greater grain-boundary density.
Grain boundaries provide nucleation sites for rapid formation of a protective chromium-rich oxide film during salt exposure.
Greater grain-boundary density promotes repair or reformation of the chromium-rich oxide film.
Unannealed coarse-grained Q235 steel forms a discontinuous and less protective oxide scale.
Annealed Q235 steel will form a more uniform and adherent chromium-enriched oxide layer than unannealed Q235 steel.
Annealed Q235 steel will undergo less corrosion-related mass change or mass loss than unannealed Q235 steel.
Annealed Q235 steel will exhibit lower corrosion current density and higher polarization resistance than unannealed Q235 steel.
The proposed grain-boundary-mediated protection will operate in aggressive salt environments at both room temperature and 700–900 °C.
The hypothesis should apply when salt-induced oxidation predominates but may fail when impurity-driven pitting or mechanical wear predominates.
Results from HEAs and stainless or related steels support the concept that microstructural refinement can enhance oxide passivation.
The quantitative effect of grain-boundary density on oxide continuity in Q235 steel across room- and high-temperature regimes remains unestablished.
